explanations.explanation: That's the job, baker. David and the commanders set these sons apart "to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals." (1 Chronicles 25:1) So the assignment is part prophecy, part band practice, and I love that combination.

explanations.answer: Guard the gates of the city
explanations.explanation: I get the guess, since army commanders are in the room. But the text says these sons were set apart to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals (1 Chronicles 25:1). Nobody hands a guard a harp and says "watch that gate." Well, maybe nobody hands them one on purpose.

Nope, no treasury shifts here. The text says they were set apart to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals (1 Chronicles 25:1). Cymbals are LOUD, and a loud treasury guard doesn't sneak up on anybody.

Right, baker. The text says Asaph "prophesied under the direction of the king." (1 Chronicles 25:2) So the sons answer to their father, and their father answers to the king. Everybody in this band has somebody to answer to.

It's actually true. The text says the sons of Asaph were under Asaph's direction, and that Asaph "prophesied under the direction of the king." (1 Chronicles 25:2) So Asaph isn't the top of the chain. Even the bandleader has a boss.

explanations.answer: Giving thanks and praise to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says Jeduthun "prophesied with the harp, giving thanks and praise to the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:3) Thanks and praise, with strings attached. Sorry, I couldn't help it.

explanations.answer: Warning the king about his enemies
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd guess that, since prophets sometimes carry hard messages. But this verse says Jeduthun prophesied with the harp "giving thanks and praise to the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:3) Nothing about enemies here. This one's all thanks.

explanations.answer: Mourning over the sins of the city
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says Jeduthun prophesied with the harp "giving thanks and praise to the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:3) A harp can sound sad, I'll give you that. But the verse tells us what he was doing, and it's thanks and praise.

You got it, baker. The text says these sons were given to Heman "through the promises of God to exalt him." (1 Chronicles 25:5) It's a promise, and the children came with it. I think that's a whole lot of reasons to smile.

Close in sound, opposite in meaning. The text says the sons were given to Heman "through the promises of God to exalt him." (1 Chronicles 25:5) Exalt means lift up, not bring down. So this is a gift, not a lesson in humility.

Good thinking, but the verse doesn't say that. It says the sons were given to Heman "through the promises of God to exalt him." (1 Chronicles 25:5) The text gives a promise and a lifting up. A test never shows up in it.

explanations.answer: The service of the house of God
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says they were under their fathers' direction "for the music of the house of the LORD…for the service of the house of God." (1 Chronicles 25:6) All those cymbals and harps were for that house. No small gig.

explanations.answer: The king's court at the palace
explanations.explanation: The king is in the picture, since Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman were under his direction. But the music itself was "for the service of the house of God." (1 Chronicles 25:6) So the stage is God's house, not the palace.

The army commanders did help set these musicians apart (1 Chronicles 25:1), so I see the thinking. But verse 6 says the music was "for the service of the house of God." The cymbals were for God's house, not a battlefield.
Yes, baker. The relatives were "all trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:7) Trained AND skillful. These folks practiced, and I'm proud of every one of them.
Laws are important, but that's not the word here. The text says the relatives were "all trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:7) This was a music crew, so it's songs.
Good guess with army commanders around, but no. The relatives were "all trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 25:7) Their training was for singing and playing, not fighting.

Not quite, baker. The text says they cast lots for their duties, "young and old alike, teacher as well as pupil." (1 Chronicles 25:8) So the teachers were right in there with everybody else. Nobody got a free pass.

Right, baker. The text says they cast lots for their duties, "young and old alike, teacher as well as pupil." (1 Chronicles 25:8) The teachers drew a lot just like the students. I think that's a good way to keep everybody on equal footing.
